prompt: From the laptop, `hq` replied with `ttl=64` and web1 with `ttl=62`. How many routers did web1's reply cross?
hint: Linux starts at 64 and each router takes one.

prompt: Fifty pings to web2 lost 12%, and the rule on the ISP drops 20% at random. What does the gap tell you?
hint: Run the arithmetic of the example.

choices.text: The rule is dropping less than it was set to
choices.why: At a true 20%, fifty pings report 12% or less in about one run in ten; the rule is fine.

choices.text: Nothing: fifty pings are too few to pin the rate
choices.why: Right. Fifty pings report anything from 10% to 32% in ninety-five runs out of a hundred.

choices.text: ping undercounts loss when the interval is short
choices.why: Each echo came back or it did not; ping counts both exactly.

choices.text: ping resent the lost echoes and some got through
choices.why: ping never resends: each sequence number is sent once.

prompt: `ping -s 1400` printed `1400(1428) bytes of data`. What are the other 28 bytes?
hint: An echo is ICMP inside IP.

choices.text: The Ethernet header and its checksum
choices.why: Ethernet is below the packet and is not in either figure.

choices.text: A TCP header and an IP header
choices.why: ping sends ICMP; there is no TCP in an echo.

choices.text: 8 of ICMP header and 20 of IP
choices.why: Right. The data plus both headers is the packet on the wire.

choices.text: Padding ping adds to round the size up
choices.why: Nothing is padded; the 28 are headers.

prompt: A server's ping replies arrive with `ttl=125`. What can you say about the path?
hint: Where did the count start?

choices.text: It is 125 routers away
choices.why: TTL counts down from a starting value; nothing starts at zero.

choices.text: Three hops, if it started at 128
choices.why: Right. Windows starts at 128, so a reply at 125 crossed three routers; TTL is a distance only once you know the start.

choices.text: The path is congested and packets are ageing
choices.why: TTL drops once per router, not with time spent in a queue.

choices.text: It is 125 milliseconds away
choices.why: TTL is a hop count here, not a time; the time is the time= field.

prompt: With `traceroute -n -q 1`, hop 2 shows `*` and hop 3, the server, answers. What do you conclude?
hint: Every probe that reached hop 3 crossed hop 2.

choices.text: Hop 2 forwards but stays quiet
choices.why: Right. Forwarding works; only the router's own time exceeded is missing.

choices.text: Hop 2 is down and traffic went round it
choices.why: There is no way round in this path, and the server answered through it.

choices.text: The server sits behind a firewall
choices.why: The server answered; the silence is at hop 2.

choices.text: The path loses packets at hop 2
choices.why: A lossy hop would lose probes to hop 3 as well, and none were lost.

prompt: How does the default Linux traceroute know that it has reached the destination?
hint: Its probes are UDP to high ports.

choices.text: The destination answers time exceeded
choices.why: Time exceeded comes from the routers before it, where the TTL runs out.

choices.text: It stops after three hops
choices.why: The limit is 30 hops, as its first line says; three is how many probes per hop.

choices.text: The destination answers port unreachable
choices.why: Right. Nothing listens on those ports, so the destination says so, and that answer ends the trace.

choices.text: The destination's reply has a TTL of zero
choices.why: A reply's TTL starts high, at 64 on Linux.

prompt: Why did `traceroute -n -T -p 80` run with `sudo`?
hint: How are the probes made?

choices.text: Port 80 is below 1024, which only root may use
choices.why: That rule is about listening on a port, not sending to one; any user can connect to port 80.

choices.text: It builds its TCP packets on a raw socket
choices.why: Right. Setting the TTL of a hand-made SYN needs a raw socket, and that needs root.

choices.text: A firewall stops ordinary users sending TCP probes
choices.why: No firewall knows which user on the laptop sent a packet.

choices.text: sudo gives the probes a higher priority
choices.why: sudo changes who runs the program, not how the network treats its packets.

prompt: Match each traceroute to what its probes are.
hint: The default is not ICMP.

pairs.right: UDP to high ports, ended by port unreachable
TCP SYNs to a port a firewall lets through

prompt: An mtr report shows 80.0% loss at hops 1 and 2, and 0.0% at the destination. What is losing packets?
hint: Read the last line first.

choices.text: hq, which drops four packets in five
choices.why: Then nothing past hq could do better than one in five, and the destination got all 50.

choices.text: The ISP router, where the loss continues
choices.why: It does not continue: the destination lost nothing.

choices.text: Nothing on the path
choices.why: Right. The routers limit their own time exceeded answers; the destination's echo reply is not limited, and all 50 came back.

choices.text: The destination, which hides its loss
choices.why: A destination cannot answer a probe it never received.

prompt: An mtr report shows 0% at hops 1 to 4, then 15% at hop 5, and 15% at hops 6 and 7, the destination. Where do you look?
hint: Where does the loss begin and stay?

choices.text: At hop 7, the destination
choices.why: The loss began two hops earlier and was carried through.

choices.text: At hop 5, or the link into it
choices.why: Right. Loss that starts at a hop and stays to the end is real, and starts there.

choices.text: Nowhere: it is ICMP rate limiting
choices.why: Rate limiting never reaches the destination; this does.

choices.text: At hop 1, because loss adds up along the path
choices.why: Hop 1 lost nothing; loss shows where it happens.

prompt: `icmp_ratemask = 6168` is 4096 + 2048 + 16 + 8. Which bit, the ICMP type every intermediate hop answers traceroute with, makes the 2048?
hint: 2048 is 2 to the power of what?

prompt: The first mtr, at one probe a second, showed 0.0% at hops 1 and 2; the second, at ten a second, showed 80.0%. Why the difference?
hint: icmp_ratelimit = 1000.

choices.text: One a second stayed inside the ICMP limit; ten did not
choices.why: Right. After a small burst each router answers one probe a second.

choices.text: Removing the drop rule created loss at the hops
choices.why: Removing a drop cannot add loss, and that rule touched only traffic to web2.

choices.text: Loss grows as more probes are sent
choices.why: A percentage does not grow with the count; 20 probes and 50 measure the same rate.

choices.text: The second run went to web1 by another path
choices.why: Both crossed hq and the ISP, the same two hops.

prompt: nslookup printed `** server can't find nosuch.example.com: NXDOMAIN`. What happened?
hint: NXDOMAIN is an rcode in a reply.

choices.text: The server could not be reached
choices.why: That prints timeouts and no servers could be reached, with no server line.

choices.text: The server answered that the name does not exist
choices.why: Right. A server was reached, looked, and said so.

choices.text: The name exists but has no address record
choices.why: That is a different answer, with no error code; NXDOMAIN says the name itself is absent.

choices.text: The laptop's resolver setting is wrong
choices.why: The configured server, 192.0.2.53, answered, so the setting worked.

prompt: Which part of nslookup's output answers the question 'was I asking the right server?'
hint: The header comes before the answer.

choices.text: `Name:`
choices.why: That repeats the name asked about.

choices.text: The `Server:` line at the top
choices.why: Right. It names the server that answered, before any answer.
That is the answer, the name's address, not who gave it.

choices.text: The last, empty line
choices.why: It ends the output and says nothing.

prompt: NXDOMAIN comes from a server that looked the name up; three timeouts mean that no ___ came back at all.
hint: The opposite of NXDOMAIN, not the same failure.

prompt: Which of iperf3's two summary lines is the throughput to quote?
hint: What arrived, not what was pushed.

choices.text: The receiver's
choices.why: Right. 19.1 Mbit/s is what reached web1.

choices.text: The sender's, the higher one
choices.why: 20.1 is what was pushed, including what had to be sent again.

choices.text: The first second, the peak
choices.why: 26.2 was TCP overshooting before the drops; it is not the path's rate.

choices.text: The average of sender and receiver
choices.why: An average of two different things is neither of them.

prompt: Upload measured 19.1 Mbit/s received and `-R` measured 3.31 Gbit/s. Why the difference?
hint: Where was the shaper?

choices.text: -R uses UDP, which the shaper ignores
choices.why: -R is still TCP; it only swaps who sends.

choices.text: Only hq's upload was shaped
choices.why: Right. The shaper sat on what leaves hq towards the ISP; the download direction had none.

choices.text: web1 sends faster than the laptop can
choices.why: Both are namespaces on one computer; the 20 Mbit/s cap is a shaper, not a machine.

choices.text: The reverse test opens four streams
choices.why: That is -P 4, and four streams made 20.8 Mbit/s, not gigabits.

prompt: `-P 4` made 20.8 Mbit/s against 20.1 for one stream. In which situation would parallel streams have raised the number?
hint: What caps the total here, and what caps one connection elsewhere?

choices.text: On any link, since four streams get four shares
choices.why: Against this shaper four streams made the same 20; the total was the limit.

choices.text: On a shaped link, to get round the shaper
choices.why: A shaper caps the total, so extra streams only split it.

choices.text: On a link that loses UDP
choices.why: -P 4 here is TCP, and loss slows TCP streams whatever their number.

choices.text: On a long path where one stream's window is the limit
choices.why: Right. Each stream has its own window, so four can fill a path one cannot.

prompt: At `-u -b 30M` the receiver got 19.5 Mbit/s and 34% loss. What did UDP do that TCP did not?
hint: TCP backs off; UDP has no mechanism to.

choices.text: It resent the lost datagrams
choices.why: UDP resends nothing; the 4432 lost stayed lost.

choices.text: It kept sending at the asked rate
choices.why: Right. It held 30 Mbit/s and nothing told it to slow down, so the shaper dropped what did not fit.

choices.text: It slowed down when jitter rose
choices.why: The sender held 30.0 Mbit/s throughout.

choices.text: It compressed the data to fit the link
choices.why: Nothing compresses here; 19.5 is what survived.

prompt: A browser speed test reads well below the plan's rate. Which of these could explain it? Choose all that apply.
hint: The test counts data, over the whole path.

choices.text: The Wi-Fi between the laptop and the router
choices.why: Right: it is part of the path the test measures.

choices.text: Headers the plan counts and the test does not
choices.why: Right: the line carries them, the test reports only data.

choices.text: ICMP rate limiting at the provider's routers
choices.why: A speed test moves data over TCP; ICMP limits never touch it.

choices.text: The test server sitting close to the provider
choices.why: A near server flatters the number; it cannot explain a low one.

prompt: A user says a site 'does not exist'. `nslookup` prints three `communications error ... timed out` lines and `no servers could be reached`. Where do you look?
hint: No server line, no answer.

choices.text: At the site's DNS record, missing from the server
choices.why: A missing record comes back as NXDOMAIN, from a server that answered.

choices.text: At the path to DNS, or the resolver setting
choices.why: Right. Nothing answered, so nothing is known about the name yet.

choices.text: At the web server, which is down
choices.why: The web server has not been reached: there is no address to reach it at.

choices.text: At the browser's cache
choices.why: nslookup never uses the browser; the failure is its own.

prompt: Put these in the order they answer 'can the laptop fetch www.example.com quickly?'
hint: A name before an address; reaching before carrying.
items: nslookup www.example.com: does the name resolve?
mtr 192.0.2.80: is anything lost on the way, and where?
iperf3 to a machine at the far end: how much does the path carry?
trap: Without a name there is no address to ping, and a throughput test on a path that loses packets measures the loss.

prompt: Which tool answers 'is anything being lost between here and web2, and at which hop?'
hint: Whether, and where, over many rounds.

choices.text: ping
choices.why: ping says whether and how much, but not at which hop.

choices.text: traceroute, run once
choices.why: Three probes a hop, once, cannot measure a rate of loss.

choices.text: mtr
choices.why: Right. It probes every hop round after round and counts the losses per hop.

choices.text: iperf3 in UDP mode
choices.why: It measures loss end to end, with no hops at all.
